Surah "Al-Mulk" (The Sovereignty)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

It is also called "Al-Waqiyah" (The Protector) and "Al-Munjiyah" (The Deliverer), because it protects its reciter from the punishment of the grave. And it has come, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites it in a night has indeed multiplied and purified (his reward)."

﴿Blessed﴾ is He, exalted and magnified above the attributes of created beings,

﴿in whose hand is the sovereignty﴾, that is: by His disposal is the dominion and the control over every existing thing, and He is the Owner of sovereignty, giving it to whomever He wills and taking it away from whomever He wills,

﴿and He is over all things﴾, of what is within the scope of power, or of bestowing favour and of exacting retribution,

﴿Competent﴾, Able to a perfect degree.

﴿Who created death﴾: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, or an apposition (*badal*) to the preceding ﴿Who﴾.

﴿and life﴾: that is, that by whose existence sensation becomes possible. Death is its opposite. The meaning of creating death and life is bringing into being that which makes sensation possible, and bringing about its non-existence. The meaning is: He created your death and your life, O accountable ones,

﴿that He may test you﴾: that He may examine you by His command and His prohibition, in the span between death, which comes to all alike, the ruler and the captive, and life, which cannot be relied upon to be spared from illness or saved by a physician. Thus what He knows will come from you becomes manifest, and He will recompense you for your deeds, not for His knowledge of you.

﴿which of you﴾: is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is ﴿is best in deed﴾, that is, the most sincere and the most correct. Sincerity is that it be for the sake of God's countenance, and correctness is that it be according to the *sunnah* (the prescribed way of the Prophet ﷺ). The meaning is that He gave you life, by which you are able to act, and subjected you to death, which calls you to choose good deeds over bad. Beyond it there is nothing but resurrection and recompense, which is unavoidable. Death was placed before life because the people most powerfully motivated to act are those who keep their death before their eyes. Death was placed first because, with respect to what the verse is addressed to, it is more important. Since He placed death, which is the effect of the attribute of dominance (*qahr*), before life, which is the effect of kindness (*lutf*), He placed the attribute of dominance before the attribute of kindness, by His saying: ﴿And He is the Mighty﴾, that is, the Overpowering, whom no one who does evil can escape,

﴿the Forgiving﴾, the Concealer, from whom those who commit evil and slip do not despair.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 67, verse 3:

﴿He who created seven heavens in layers (ṭibāqan)﴾, i.e., corresponding to one another, one above another. It is derived from "ṭābaqa al-naʿl" (he fitted the sandal), when he stitched it, layer upon layer. This is a description using the verbal noun (maṣdar), or it is taken as "dhāta ṭibāq" (possessing layers), or as "ṭūbiqat ṭibāqan" (they were made into layers). It has also been said that it is the plural of "ṭabaq" (layer), like "jamal" (camel) and "jimāl" (camels). The address in ﴿You see no disparity in the creation of the Most Merciful﴾ is to the Messenger, or to every addressee.

﴿Disparity (min tafāwut)﴾: it is read as "min tafawwut" by Ḥamzah and ʿAlī, and the two patterns have the same meaning, like "al-taʿāhud" and "al-taʿahhud" (mutual covenant). That is: from discord and disorder. And from al-Suddi: "from defect." The real meaning of tafāwut is lack of proportion, as if some part of a thing fails to match another part and does not suit it. This clause is a description of "ṭibāqan," and its original form is: "You see in them no disparity." The phrase ﴿the creation of the Most Merciful﴾ was placed in the position of the pronoun, to magnify their creation and to draw attention to the reason for their being free of disparity: that it is the creation of the Most Merciful, and that He, by the dazzling power of His ability, is the One who creates the like of that proportionate creation.

﴿Then return the gaze﴾: turn it back to the sky, until what you were informed of is confirmed for you by direct observation, so that no doubt about it remains with you.

﴿Do you see any rifts (fuṭūr)?﴾: cracks and fissures. It is the plural of "fatr," which is a split.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 67, verse 4:

﴿Then return your gaze twice﴾: repeat the looking twice, i.e., two times in addition to the first. It was also said: "in addition to the first," so that it makes three times. It was also said: He did not intend to limit it to two, but intended repetition in great number, i.e., "Repeat your look and scrutinize it: do you see any flaw or defect?" The response to the command is: ﴿it will return to you﴾, meaning, it will come back to you,

﴿the gaze, humbled﴾, meaning, disgraced, or far from what you desire; it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "al-baṣar" (the gaze),

﴿while it is exhausted﴾, meaning, worn out, tired, and it has seen no flaw in it.

Indeed, We have adorned the nearest heaven, that is, the lowest heaven, the one nearest to you,

with lamps, meaning shining stars, like the brightness of the dawn. Al-masabih (المصابيح) means al-suruj (السُّرُج, lamps), and the stars were named after them. People adorn their mosques and houses by lighting lamps. "And We have indeed adorned the roof of the house in which you have gathered with lamps." That is, with what lamps! Your lamps cannot match its brightness.

And We made them missiles against the devils, that is, against your enemies who draw you out of the light into darkness. Qatada said: "God created the stars for three purposes: as an adornment for the heaven, as missiles against the devils, and as signs by which one is guided. Whoever interprets them otherwise has burdened himself with what he has no knowledge of." Al-rujum (الرُّجُوم, missiles) is the plural of rajm (رَجْم), a verbal noun used to name that with which one pelts. The meaning of their being missiles against the devils is that a shihab (شِهاب, a shooting flame) detaches from them like a firebrand taken from a fire, and it kills the jinn or disables him. This is because the stars do not leave their places, for they remain fixed in their orbit in their state.

And We have prepared for them, for the devils,

the punishment of the Blaze, in the Hereafter, after being burned by the shooting flames in this world.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 67, verse 6:**

﴿And for those who disbelieve in their Lord⦆ — and for every one who disbelieves in Allah, of the devils and others.

﴿is the punishment of Jahannam⦆ — the devils who were stoned are not specifically meant by this.

﴿and wretched is the destination⦆ — al-masir (the destination, the place of return) is Jahannam.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 67, verse 7:

﴿When they are thrown into it﴾: they are cast into Jahannam, just as firewood is cast into a great fire.

﴿they hear from it﴾: from Jahannam,

﴿a roaring (shahiq)﴾: a hideous sound, like the braying of donkeys. He likened its dreadful, terrible rumbling (hasis) to a shahiq.

﴿while it boils over﴾: it seethes with them, like a cauldron (mirjal) seething with what is in it.

Tafsir of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 67, verse 8:

﴿Takādu tamayyazu﴾ (it nearly bursts apart): i.e., it splits apart, meaning it breaks into pieces and scatters,

﴿min al-ghayz﴾ (from rage) against the disbelievers, so it is treated as one who is enraged against them, as a metaphor for the intensity of its seething over them,

﴿kullamā ulqiya fīhā fawj﴾ (every time a company is thrown into it): a group of the disbelievers,

﴿sa'alahum khazanatuhā﴾ (its guardians asked them): Mālik, and his assistants from the Zabāniyah (angels of punishment), as a rebuke to them,

﴿alam ya'tikum nadhīr﴾ (Did there not come to you a warner?): a messenger who warned you of this punishment?!

They say, "Yes, indeed, a warner did come to us," an acknowledgment from them of God's justice, and an affirmation that He (exalted is He) removed their excuse by sending the Messengers and warning them of what they had fallen into.

﴿So we denied﴾, i.e., we denied them.

﴿And we said, "God has not sent down anything,"﴾ of what you say, of promise and threat and other things.

﴿"You are only in great error."﴾ i.e., the disbelievers said to the warners: "You are only in a grave mistake." So "nadhir" (warner) is used with the meaning of "al-infar" (warning), and then their warners were described by it, due to their excessiveness in warning, as if they were nothing but warning. It is also permissible that this is the speech of the guardians of Hell (al-khazanah) to the disbelievers, on the assumption of an implied "they say." Their meaning by "error" is "destruction." Or they named the recompense of error by its name, as the recompense of an evil deed and of transgression is called "an evil deed" and "transgression," and this is called "al-mushakalah" (figure of likeness) in the science of rhetoric. Or it is the speech of the Messengers to them, which they relayed to the guardians, meaning: "They said this to us, but we did not accept it."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 67, verse 10:

﴿And they will say: "Had we been listening"﴾, to the warning, listening as one seeking the truth,

﴿or using our reason﴾, i.e., using our reason for it, reasoning as one who reflects,

﴿we would not have been among the companions of the Blaze﴾, among the people of the Fire. In this is evidence that the basis of moral obligation (taklif) rests upon the proofs of revelation (sam') and reason ('aql), and that these two are binding proofs (hujjatan mulzimatan).

﴿So they will acknowledge their sin﴾, that is, their disbelief in denying the messengers,

﴿So away with the companions of the Blaze!﴾ The reading of "suḥqan" with a ḍammah on the ḥā' is that of Yazīd and ʿAlī (ibn Ḥamzah? no — rendered as in the source: Yazīd and ʿAlī). Meaning: far away from them from the mercy of Allah and His honour. Whether they acknowledge or deny [their sin], that will not benefit them. Its grammatical position (inṣāb) is that it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) that stands in the place of an invocation (duʿāʾ).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 67, verse 12:

﴿Indeed, those who fear their Lord unseen⁠—﴾ before witnessing the punishment,

﴿for them is forgiveness﴾ of sins,

﴿and a great reward﴾, i.e., Paradise.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 67, verse 13:

﴿And keep your speech secret or declare it aloud﴾. Its apparent meaning is a command to do one of two things: to keep it secret, or to declare it aloud. Its meaning is: let your secrecy and your declaring be alike in the knowledge of Allah concerning them both. It is narrated (p-514) that the polytheists of Mecca used to revile the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and Jibril would inform him of what they had said about him and the abuse they had heaped upon him. They said among themselves: "Keep your speech secret, lest the god of Muhammad hear it." So this verse was revealed. It was then given a reason by His words: ﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is in the breasts﴾, that is, of what is in their inner selves, before the tongues translate them. So how could He not know what has been spoken?

Ala ya'lamu man khalaq (Does not He who created know?): "man" is in the nominative position as the subject (fa'il) of "ya'lamu."

Wa huwa al-latif al-khabir (while He is the Subtle, the All-Aware): He denied that the One who created them would not have comprehensive knowledge of what is concealed, what is hidden, and what is openly declared. His attribute is that He is al-Latif, meaning the One who knows the subtleties of things, and al-Khabir, the One who knows the realities of things. In this there is an affirmation of the creation of speech, and so it serves as evidence for the creation of the actions of servants. Abu Bakr ibn al-Asamm and Ja'far ibn Harb said: "man" is the object (maf'ul), and the subject is a pronoun (mudmar) referring to Allah (exalted is He). By this they sought to negate the creation of actions.

**He is Allah**,

**"who has made the earth tractable for you"** (ذَلُولا, *dhalūl*): soft, easy, made docile, not preventing walking upon it.

**"So walk in its broad paths"** (فِي مَنَاكِبِهَا, *fī manākibihā*): its sides and regions, for reflection and for seeking provision; or its mountains, or its roads.

**"And eat of His provision"**: that is, of the provision of Allah in it.

**"And to Him is the resurrection"**: that is, to Him is your resurrection, and so He will call you to account for thanking Him for what He has bestowed upon you.

Are you secure from He who is in the heaven? That is: He whose dominion is in the heaven, because it is the dwelling place of His angels, and from it His decrees, His books, His commands and His prohibitions descend. So it is as if He said: "Are you secure from the Creator of the heaven and its Sovereign?!" Or, because they used to hold the doctrine of anthropomorphism (tashbih), that He is in the heaven, and that mercy and punishment descend from Him, so it was said to them, according to their own belief: "Are you secure from the One whom you claim to be in the heaven?!" — whereas He is exalted above place.

﴿Lest He cause the earth to swallow you up,﴾ as He caused Qarun to be swallowed up,

﴿and behold, it quakes.﴾ That is, it is agitated and moves.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 67, verse 17:

﴿Or do you feel secure from the One in heaven that He will not send against you a violent wind of stones?﴾ "Hasiban" means stones. "An yursila" is a substitute (badal) for "man," a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal), and likewise "an yakhsifa,"

﴿So you will know how My warning was﴾ meaning: when you see the threatened punishment (al-mundhar bihi), you will know how My warning was, at a time when knowledge will not benefit you. (p-515)

And those before them denied, from before your people, ﴿so how was My denunciation?﴾ That is, My disapproval of them when I destroyed them. Then He drew attention to His power to cause the earth to swallow up (al-khasf) and to send down a hurling storm (al-hasib), by His saying:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 67, verse 19:

﴿Have they not seen the birds above them⁠—﴾, plural of "ṭā'ir" (bird),

﴿above them﴾, in the air,

﴿spreading their wings⁠—﴾, extending their wings in the air, during their flight,

﴿and folding them in﴾, gathering them in when they strike their sides with them. "And folding them in" is coordinated with the active participle (ism al-fā'il) by way of taking account of meaning (ḥamlan 'alā al-ma'nā), i.e., "arranging themselves and folding," or "spreading and folding." The choice of this construction is based on the fact that the basic nature of flight is the spreading of the wings, because flying in the air is like swimming in water, and the air is to the bird what water is to the swimmer. The basic form of swimming is the extending and stretching of the limbs, whereas folding is something that occurs after spreading, to gain support for movement. Thus what is secondary is expressed by the verb, with the meaning that they are spreading, and folding occurs from them at times after times, just as it occurs from the swimmer.

﴿What holds them up﴾, from falling during folding and spreading,

﴿except the Most Merciful﴾, by His power. Otherwise, the heavy thing would by nature sink and not rise. Likewise, if He withheld His preservation and management from the world, the heavens would collapse. "What holds them up" is a new sentence (mustanaf'anaf), though it is permissible to take it as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "folding them in."

﴿Indeed He is, of everything, All-Seeing﴾, He knows how to create and how to manage wonders.

"Am man" (or "Am man," the interrogative "or who"), a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is: ﴿hadha﴾ (this). And ﴿alladhi huwa jundun lakum﴾ (he who is a host for you) is put in apposition (badal) to "hadha" (this). The position (mahall) of ﴿yansurukum min duni l-Rahman﴾ (who will help you apart from the All-Merciful) is nominative (raf'), as a qualifying adjective (na't) of "jund" (host), treated according to its wording (mahmul 'ala l-lafz). The meaning is: "Who is the one indicated as the helper, other than Allah (Exalted)?!"

﴿in al-kafiruna illa fi ghurur﴾ (The disbelievers are only in delusion), i.e., they are nothing but in delusion.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 67, verse 21:

﴿Who is this that could provide for you if He withheld His provision?﴾, "Or is it one who is pointed to and it is said: 'This is the one who provides for you, if He withholds His provision?!'" This is according to the estimation (al-taqdir). It is also permissible that it be a reference to all the idols (al-awthan), because of their belief that they protect from calamities and provide sustenance through the blessing of their gods. So it is as if they were the helping army and the provider. When they did not take heed, He turned away from them and said: ﴿Nay, they persist﴾, they persevere (tamadaw),

﴿in arrogance﴾, pride (istikbar) against the truth,

﴿and aversion﴾, and fleeing from it (shirad 'anhu), because it was burdensome to them, so they did not follow it. Then He set forth an example for the disbelievers and the believers, and said:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 67, verse 22:

﴿Is one who walks prone on his face better guided?﴾ That is: fallen upon his face, stumbling at every moment, walking in a headlong and uneven manner. The predicate of "man" (man, "one who") is ﴿better guided﴾ (ahdā, "more rightly guided"). Here "ukibba" (أُكِبَّ, "he was made to fall prone") is the reflexive form (muṭāwaʿ) of "kabbahu" (كَبَّهُ, "he made him fall prone"); it is said: "I made him fall prone (kababtuhu), so he fell prone (ukibba)."

﴿Or one who walks upright﴾ (sawiyyan, "level, erect"), standing straight, safe from stumbling and falling,

﴿on a straight path﴾, on a level road. The predicate of "man" here is omitted, because "ahdā" (better guided) indicates it.

It is related from al-Kalbi: "By the one who is prone (al-mukibb) is meant Abu Jahl, and by the one who is upright (al-sawiyy) is meant the Prophet (ﷺ)."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 67, verse 23:

﴿Say: He it is Who brought you into being⁠⁠—﴾ He created you originally (khalaqakum ibtida'an),

﴿and made for you hearing, sight and hearts⁠⁠—﴾ He singled them out, because they are the instruments of knowledge (alat al-'ilm),

﴿little thanks do you give.⁠⁠—﴾ for these blessings, because you associate partners with Allah and do not devote worship sincerely to Him. The meaning is: you give thanks, but a little thanks. And "ma" is superfluous (za'idah). It has also been said: "little" (al-qillah) is an expression for non-existence (al-'adam).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 67, verse 24:

﴿Say: It is He who created you﴾, that is, brought you into being (khalaqakum),

﴿on the earth, and to Him you will be gathered﴾, for reckoning and recompense (lil-hisab wal-jaza').

And they say, that is, the disbelievers, to the believers, mockingly:

"When is this promise," which you make to us, meaning the punishment,

"if you are truthful," about its occurring? So inform us of its time.

﴿Say: "The knowledge is only with Allah"﴾, that is, the knowledge of the time of the punishment,

﴿and I am only a warner﴾, one who instills fear,

﴿clear﴾, I make the laws (sharā'i') clear to you.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 67, verse 27:

﴿When they see it﴾, i.e., the promise, meaning the promised punishment,

﴿approaching﴾, near to them. Its case (intisab) is that of a circumstantial accusative (hal).

﴿The faces of those who disbelieved will be distressed﴾, i.e., the sight of the promise will distress their faces, so that dejection and grief will overcome them, and blackness and gloom will cover them.

﴿And it will be said: This is what you used to call for﴾, the speakers being the guardians of Hell (al-zabaniyah).

﴿Kuntum bihi tadda'un﴾, "tafta'ilun" (the form tadda'un, from the verb ta-fa'ala, reflexive/reciprocal pattern), from "al-du'a'" (calling, supplication), meaning: you used to ask for its hastening and say: "Bring us what you promise us." Or it is from "al-da'wa" (claim), meaning: you used to claim, because of it, that you would not be resurrected. Ya'qub recited it as "tad'una" (without the doubled letter).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 67, verse 28:

﴿Say: "Have you considered: if Allah destroys me and those with me, or has mercy upon us, who will protect the disbelievers from a painful punishment?"﴾ That is: if Allah causes me to die, as in His saying: ﴿If a man dies [and has no offspring]﴾ [al-Nisa': 176]. ﴿And those with me﴾, from among my companions,

﴿or has mercy upon us﴾, or postpones our term (ajal, the appointed term of life),

﴿who will protect﴾, who will save,

﴿the disbelievers from a painful punishment﴾, a punishing one. The disbelievers of Makkah used to pray against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and against the believers that they be destroyed, so he was commanded to say to them: "We are believers, awaiting one of the two good outcomes (al-husnayayn). Either we die as you wish, and we return to Paradise, or we are shown mercy through victory over you, as we hope. So what will you do? Who will protect you, while you are disbelievers, from the punishment of the Fire?! You must face it."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 67, verse 29:

﴿Say: He is the Most Merciful (al-Rahman)﴾, i.e., the One to whom I invite you is al-Rahman,

﴿We have believed in Him﴾, we have affirmed Him, and we have not disbelieved in Him as you have disbelieved,

﴿and in Him we have put our trust﴾, we have entrusted our affairs to Him,

﴿so you will come to know﴾, when the punishment descends upon you, and with the yā' (as a reading) "ʿAlī" ("so he will come to know"), ﴿who is in manifest error﴾, whether we or you.

﴿Say: "Tell me, if your water should become sunken (ghawran)"﴾, meaning: disappeared, sinking into the earth, out of reach of buckets. It is a description using the verbal noun (maṣdar), like "ʿadl" (justice) in the sense of "ʿādil" (just).

﴿then who will bring you flowing water (māʾun maʿīn)?﴾ meaning: flowing, which reaches whoever seeks it. It was recited in the presence of a heretic (mulḥid), and he said: "It brings it with the pickaxe and the helper (al-miʿwal wal-muʿīn)." That night the water of his eye went away, and he became blind. It is said that he was Muḥammad ibn Zakariyyā al-Mutaṭabbib (the physician). May Allah increase us in insight.
